sections.heading: Images live in a Regional ECR repository that tasks pull from

plan.problem: A team builds an image on a laptop. Tasks in two Regions must start from that image, and a released tag must never change.
trace: **Log in.** The Docker CLI [doesn't support native IAM authentication methods] (ecr-docker-cli-needs-token-get-login-password), so the client gets an authorization token that is valid for [12 hours] (ecr-authorization-token-valid-12-hours).

**Push.** The image goes into a repository, [a logical collection where you can store] images (ecr-repository-logical-collection-of-images); each account has [a default private Amazon ECR registry] (ecr-default-private-registry-per-account) in each Region.

**Store.** ECR encrypts the image with [server-side encryption with Amazon S3-managed encryption keys] (ecr-encryption-default-sse-s3-aes256); with tag immutability you [prevent image tags from being overwritten] (ecr-tag-immutability-prevent-overwrite).
**Pull.** A task in the same Region pulls the image, and that transfer [is free of charge] (ecr-pricing-same-region-transfer-free).
plan.table_note: No table: the trace has one case. The two-Region case goes into the Why and the Exam trap.
plan.why: Why one repository per Region? ECR is a [Regional service] (ecr-faq-regional-service): a pull from another Region adds [additional latency and data transfer costs] (ecr-faq-cross-region-pull-latency-and-transfer-cost), so AWS says to [Host your images in a repository] in the Region of the workload (ecs-keep-images-in-same-region-as-workload).
plan.exam_signal: "scan each new image for vulnerabilities when it is pushed" points to scan on push, which scans [each new image pushed to the repository] (ecr-scan-on-push-each-new-image); "continuous scanning, including programming language packages" points to enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector: [automated, continuous scanning of your repositories] (ecr-scanning-basic-vs-enhanced).
plan.exam_trap_text: Wrong belief: one repository in the first Region serves tasks in every Region. Truth: ECR can [automatically replicate them to other Regions and accounts] (ecr-faq-replicates-across-regions-and-accounts), so each Region pulls locally. End with <!-- trap: containers-trap-ecr-global -->. At most 40 words.
plan.try_it: Try it callout for containers-t02 after the Exam trap, ending with its task comment.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: sharing, caching and cleaning up images (at most 65 words). By default [only the AWS account that created the repository] has access (ecr-repository-policy-default-account-only); for cross-account replication [The source account does not require] a policy (ecr-replication-destination-account-policy-only). A pull through cache rule lets ECR [cache repositories in an upstream registry] (ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current); after a one-time copy, newer versions [are not pulled automatically] (ecr-migrate-one-time-copy-no-auto-update). A lifecycle policy expires images [older than the specified number of days] (ecr-lifecycle-count-more-than-and-since-pushed), and you pay for [the amount of data you store] (ecr-faq-pricing-storage-and-internet-transfer).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: push each image to ECR in the Region where it runs. The thing to watch is a second Region.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team turns on replication to a second Region for a repository that already holds 40 images. An hour later, the second Region pulls the release tag that was pushed last week. Does the pull work? Answer: no; only content pushed [after replication is configured is replicated] (ecr-replication-only-new-pushes); push the tag again or copy it. Keep this fact out of the trace and the Go deeper.

sections.heading: A task definition gives the agent one role and the application another

plan.problem: A new task must pull a private image, send its logs, and let the application write to an S3 bucket. Two different programs make these calls.
trace: **Describe.** A task definition is [a text file in JSON format] (ecs-task-definition-json-blueprint) with up to [10 container definitions] (ecs-containers-per-task-definition-limit) and the roles of the task.

**Start.** A task is [the instantiation of a task definition] (ecs-task-is-instantiation-of-task-definition); the containers of one Fargate task [always run on the same host] (fargate-task-containers-share-resources).

**Pull and log.** The task execution role [grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents] permission to call AWS (ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents), for example to pull from [an Amazon ECR private repository] or to use [the `awslogs` log driver] (ecs-task-execution-role-use-cases).

**Run the code.** The task role [allows your application code (running in the container)] to call services such as Amazon S3 (ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions); the SDK uses the credentials [provided by the task role exclusively] (ecs-task-role-credentials-exclusive-no-instance-inheritance).
plan.table: Which role answers which call (columns: Call | Made by | Role): pull the image from Amazon ECR | the Fargate or container agent | task execution role; send logs with the awslogs driver | the agent | task execution role; read a secret that the task definition names | the agent | task execution role: it [references sensitive data using Secrets Manager secrets] (ecs-task-execution-role-use-cases); write to Amazon S3 | the application | task role: [Your application accesses other AWS services] (ecs-iam-role-table-task-role). Four rows; cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why two roles? The agent calls AWS before your code starts, and the code calls AWS while it runs. The execution role's permissions [aren't directly accessible by the containers] (ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents), so the code cannot use them.
plan.exam_signal: "the application in the container needs access to an S3 bucket" points to the task role ([use other AWS services], ecs-iam-role-table-task-role); "tasks fail because they cannot pull the image from a private repository" points to the task execution role (ecs-task-execution-role-use-cases).
plan.exam_trap_note: No Exam trap callout here: containers-trap-execution-role-for-app lives in the fast Traps list. Do not repeat it as a callout.
plan.body_extras: One sentence only if words remain: on Fargate, [EC2 instance profiles are not available] for containers (ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile); on EC2, the container instance role lets instances [register with the cluster] (ecs-iam-role-table-container-instance-role).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the agent uses the execution role, and your code uses the task role. The thing to watch is which program makes the call.
plan.stop_and_answer: The search and billing services share one task definition. Its task role can read the billing table and the audio bucket, but search needs only the bucket. What do you change? Answer: give each service its own family, each [for only one business purpose] (ecs-one-task-definition-family-per-business-purpose), and [a role for each specific task definition] with the minimum permissions (ecs-task-role-least-privilege-per-task-definition). Keep these facts out of the trace.

sections.heading: Fargate gives each task its own isolated compute and no instance to manage

plan.problem: A team wants containers without instances to patch. Before it moves, it asks what it gives up.
trace: **Ask for a size.** The task asks for vCPU and memory, and you no longer [provision, configure, or scale clusters] of instances (fargate-no-provision-vm-clusters).

**Isolate.** Each task runs on [its own single use, single tenant compute instance] (fargate-faq-single-tenant-instance-per-workload) and [does not share the underlying kernel] with another task (fargate-task-isolation-boundary).

**Patch.** AWS [is responsible for maintaining the underlying infrastructure]; when a platform revision is replaced, [all tasks running on that revision are stopped] (fargate-task-retirement-aws-maintains-infrastructure), and [the Amazon ECS scheduler automatically replaces the tasks] of a service (fargate-retirement-service-tasks-replaced-automatically).
**Bill.** You pay for the requested vCPU and memory from the image pull, [rounded up to the nearest second] (ecs-faq-fargate-billing-granularity).
plan.table: Three places for ECS tasks (columns: Question | Fargate | EC2 instances | ECS Managed Instances): Who manages the instances | AWS | you: [including instance selection, configuration, and maintenance] (ecs-cluster-ec2-full-control-you-manage-instances) | AWS: [AWS handles provisioning, scaling, patching, and maintenance] (ecs-managed-instances-full-range-ec2-aws-manages); Tasks on one host | one task (no link needed) | many: [there is no task isolation] (ecs-containers-not-security-boundary-use-fargate-for-isolation) | [multiple tasks on a single instance by default] (ecs-managed-instances-multi-task-placement-default); GPUs | [not supported on AWS Fargate today] (fargate-faq-gpu-not-supported) | yes: [root access to the operating system] is yours (ecs-faq-ec2-root-access-to-os) | yes: [GPU acceleration] (ecs-capacity-managed-instances); You pay for | each task | the instances | the instances plus a [management fee per instance, not per task] (ecs-faq-mi-compute-in-your-account-billing). Cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why can AWS patch Fargate for you? AWS owns the host, and Fargate [prevents containers from accessing the underlying host] (fargate-containers-cannot-access-host-resources). The same design removes privileged containers and host access.
plan.exam_signal: "strict isolation between tasks" points to Fargate: [For workloads with strict isolation requirements, use Fargate] (ecs-containers-not-security-boundary-use-fargate-for-isolation); "control of the instances, their operating system or their GPUs" points to EC2 capacity for customers who need [greater control of their EC2 instances] (ecs-faq-ec2-for-greater-control).
plan.exam_trap_text: Wrong belief: files that a task writes to its own storage are still there for the replacement task. Truth: a Fargate task gets [20 GiB] of ephemeral storage, and the data is erased when the workload stops (fargate-faq-ephemeral-storage-20-gib-erased); shared, lasting files go to [Amazon Elastic File System (EFS)] (fargate-faq-efs-for-persistent-storage). End with <!-- trap: containers-trap-task-storage-persists -->. At most 45 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Fargate gives each task its own compute, and AWS patches it. The thing to watch is that you lose host access.
plan.stop_and_answer: A nightly report runs as a standalone Fargate task, not in a service. AWS retires its platform revision on the night of the run. What happens to the report? Answer: AWS stops the task, and [Amazon ECS doesn’t launch a replacement task] for a standalone task (fargate-retirement-service-tasks-replaced-automatically); the team reruns it. The trace names only service tasks; keep the standalone half out of it.

sections.heading: In awsvpc mode each task gets its own network interface

plan.problem: A task in a private subnet must take requests from a load balancer and pull its image. The subnet has no route to the internet.
trace: **Attach.** Fargate tasks [require the `awsvpc` network mode], which [provides each task with an elastic network interface] (fargate-requires-awsvpc-network-mode).

**Place.** The service names subnets and [one or more security groups] (fargate-awsvpc-needs-subnets-and-security-groups), and the tasks [receive an IP address from the configured subnet] (fargate-network-security-groups-nacls-ip-from-subnet).
**Receive.** The load balancer sends requests to the task's address, so [you must choose `ip` as the target type] (fargate-target-group-ip-target-type).

**Pull.** To pull its image, the task [must have a route to the internet] (fargate-task-has-route-to-internet-to-pull), or the VPC has endpoints that keep the traffic [to the Amazon network] (ecr-privatelink-no-internet-gateway-needed).
plan.trace_note: Step 2: link [one or more security groups] (fargate-awsvpc-needs-subnets-and-security-groups) and [receive an IP address from the configured subnet] (fargate-network-security-groups-nacls-ip-from-subnet); write the step so that both displays read as part of the sentence.
plan.table: How a task gets its image (columns: Subnet | What the task needs): public subnet | [a public IP address needs to be assigned] (fargate-public-subnet-image-pull-needs-public-ip); private subnet with internet access | a route through a NAT gateway: [the subnet can have a NAT gateway attached] (fargate-task-has-route-to-internet-to-pull); private subnet with no internet access | VPC endpoints: tasks [require both Amazon ECR VPC endpoints] and [the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint] (ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3).
plan.why: Why ip targets? The task, not an instance, owns the network interface. Registering by IP address also means each container [can now have its own security group] (elb-nlb-faq-ip-targets-container-security-groups-same-port).
plan.exam_signal: "each task must have its own security group" points to awsvpc mode, which lets you use security groups [at a more granular level within your tasks] (ecs-awsvpc-task-own-eni-security-groups); "tasks in private subnets with no internet access pull images from Amazon ECR" points to VPC endpoints (ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3).
plan.exam_trap_text: Wrong belief: a target group of type instance works for Fargate tasks, as it does for EC2 instances. Truth: the tasks are [associated with an elastic network interface] and not an EC2 instance, so [you must choose `ip` as the target type] (fargate-target-group-ip-target-type). Link one display only if the second repeats the trace; at most 40 words. End with <!-- trap: containers-trap-instance-target-type -->.
plan.try_it: Try it callout for containers-t03 only if the tasks writer ships it (after the Exam trap), ending with its task comment. If containers-t03 is parked, leave the callout out.
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug (the one of the file), after the Exam trap and before the Say it, about 50 words with its reveal: 'A service runs Fargate tasks in private subnets with no NAT gateway. The team creates interface VPC endpoints for the ECR API and the Docker registry, and their security group allows port 443 from the private subnets. The tasks still fail to pull the image. What is wrong?' Reveal: the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint is missing: tasks [require both Amazon ECR VPC endpoints] and [the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint] (ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3). The port 443 rule is right ([must allow incoming connections on port 443], ecr-vpc-endpoint-security-group-port-443) and is the decoy.

sections.heading: A service keeps the desired task count and replaces tasks during a release

plan.problem: A web service must keep three tasks across Availability Zones, replace a task that fails, and ship a new version without dropping requests.
trace: **Keep the count.** A service runs and [maintain a specified number of instances] of a task definition (ecs-service-maintains-desired-count); by default the scheduler [spreads tasks across Availability Zones] (ecs-replica-strategy-default-spreads-azs).

**Replace.** The scheduler replaces a task after a [container health check] or a [load balancer target group health check] fails (ecs-service-scheduler-replaces-unhealthy-tasks), and it [automatically register and deregister your containers] with the load balancer (ecs-faq-service-scheduler-registers-containers-with-load-balancer).

**Roll out.** A rolling update [replaces the currently running tasks with new tasks] (ecs-rolling-update-replaces-tasks); by default the minimum healthy percent is [100%] (ecs-rolling-minimum-healthy-percent-default-100) and the maximum percent is [200%] (ecs-rolling-maximum-percent-default-200).

**Stop a bad release.** The deployment circuit breaker [determines if the tasks reach a steady state] and can [automatically roll back a failed deployment] (ecs-circuit-breaker-rolls-back-to-completed).
plan.trace_note: Step 1 'run and [maintain ...]': write the sentence so that the display reads naturally, for example 'A service exists to [maintain a specified number of instances] of a task definition'.
plan.table: Two ways to release (columns: Release | During the release | Undo): rolling update | old and new tasks run between the lower and the upper limit | the circuit breaker can [automatically roll back a failed deployment] (ecs-circuit-breaker-rolls-back-to-completed); blue/green | [two identical production environments called blue and green] (ecs-blue-green-definition-and-zero-downtime), which [may double your resource usage during deployments] (ecs-blue-green-doubles-resource-usage) | traffic moves back to blue. Link each fact once in the subsection: if the circuit-breaker display is in the trace, the table cell says 'circuit breaker rollback' without a link.
plan.why: Why start new tasks first? The minimum healthy percent is the [lower limit on the number of tasks] (ecs-minimum-healthy-percent-meaning) that must stay healthy; at the default, capacity never drops during a release, and the maximum percent gives the room for the new tasks.
plan.exam_signal: "test the new version before production traffic moves, and roll back fast" points to a blue/green deployment, now [part of the Amazon ECS service itself] (ecs-blue-green-native-similar-to-codedeploy); "stop the deployment when new tasks cannot start" points to the circuit breaker, which can [stop a deployment when the tasks can't start] (ecs-failed-deployment-detection-circuit-breaker-vs-alarms).

plan.say_it: The short answer is: a service keeps the count and replaces tasks that fail. The thing to watch is where it finds room for new tasks.
plan.stop_and_answer: A service has four tasks. To save money during releases, the team sets the minimum healthy percent to 50 and the maximum percent to 100. What can the scheduler do first in a release? Answer: it can [stop two existing tasks] before it starts two new tasks (ecs-min-healthy-percent-example-50-of-four), so capacity drops by half during the release. Keep this fact out of the trace.

sections.heading: Service auto scaling changes the task count and capacity providers supply the compute

plan.problem: Traffic doubles every weekday morning. The service needs more tasks, and on EC2 capacity the tasks also need more instances to run on.
trace: **Count tasks.** Service auto scaling uses Application Auto Scaling to [increase or decrease the desired number] of tasks (ecs-service-auto-scaling-application-auto-scaling), for example toward [a target value for a specific metric] such as average CPU (ecs-service-auto-scaling-types-target-step-scheduled-predictive).

**Choose capacity.** A capacity provider strategy lists providers with [the `base` and `weight` to assign to them] (ecs-capacity-provider-manages-infrastructure-scaling); FARGATE and FARGATE_SPOT are [managed by Amazon ECS on every cluster] (ecs-fargate-capacity-providers-auto-created).

**Add instances.** On EC2, managed scaling of an Auto Scaling group capacity provider lets ECS [manage the scaling of Amazon EC2 instances] (ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider), so the group can [launch EC2 instances, and then register them] (ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-reservation-above-or-below-target).

**Lose Spot.** A Fargate Spot task gets a [two-minute warning] (fargate-spot-two-minute-interruption-warning), delivered as a [SIGTERM signal to the running task] (fargate-spot-warning-delivery-sigterm-eventbridge); [Fargate doesn't replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity] (fargate-spot-no-on-demand-replacement).
plan.trace_note: Step 4 links three facts, each with its own display; if the body passes 175 words, move the SIGTERM clause into the Say it or drop it (fargate-spot-container-must-handle-sigterm stays for the speak item).
plan.table: What scales what (columns: Layer | Scaled by | Applies to): tasks | service auto scaling | services on Fargate and on EC2; EC2 instances | cluster auto scaling (managed scaling) | Auto Scaling group capacity providers; Fargate compute | AWS: [AWS manages and automatically scales the underlying capacity] (ecs-predictive-scaling-service-level-not-compute) | Fargate and Fargate Spot.
plan.why: Why two layers? Tasks and instances are different resources: a task needs room, and an instance gives room. On Fargate the second layer is AWS's job, so you scale only the tasks.
plan.exam_signal: "scale the workers on the messages waiting in an SQS queue" points to backlog per task, because queue depth is [not a reliable metric to scale on directly] (ecs-sqs-scale-on-backlog-per-task); "traffic rises at the same time every weekday" points to predictive scaling, which can [analyze daily or weekly patterns] (ecs-predictive-scaling-historical-patterns).

Truth: it changes only the task count; instances follow when an Auto Scaling group capacity provider lets ECS [manage the scaling of Amazon EC2 instances] (ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider). If that display is already in the trace, link the managed termination protection fact instead: ECS terminates only instances that [don't have any running Amazon ECS tasks] (ecs-managed-termination-protection-only-empty-instances). End with <!-- trap: containers-trap-service-scaling-adds-instances -->. At most 45 words.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: service auto scaling counts tasks, and capacity providers bring the compute. The thing to watch is Spot capacity that comes back late.
plan.stop_and_answer: A small service runs one task, on Fargate Spot only. AWS reclaims the Spot capacity. What happens to the service? Answer: [A service with only one task is interrupted] until capacity is available (fargate-spot-single-task-service-interrupted); give it a FARGATE base or more tasks. traps.belief: The task execution role gives the application in the container its permissions, for example to read an S3 bucket.
traps.truth: The task execution role is for the ECS container and Fargate agents, and its permissions are not directly accessible by the containers; the application uses the task role.

traps.belief: Fargate runs any container that EC2 capacity runs, including privileged containers, GPU work and one daemon task on every host.
traps.truth: Privileged containers are unavailable on Fargate, GPU workloads are not supported there, and Fargate does not support the DAEMON scheduling strategy.

traps.belief: When Fargate Spot capacity is not available, ECS starts the tasks on regular Fargate instead.
traps.truth: Fargate does not replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity; a capacity provider strategy with a base on FARGATE keeps a minimum running.

traps.belief: One ECR repository in one Region serves tasks in every Region at no extra cost.
traps.truth: ECR is a Regional service; pulls from another Region add latency and data transfer costs, and replication copies images to other Regions.

traps.belief: Files that a task writes to its own storage are still there for the task that replaces it.
traps.truth: Fargate ephemeral storage is erased when the workload stops, and an EBS volume of a service task is deleted at task termination; shared, lasting files go to Amazon EFS.

traps.belief: A target group of type instance works for Fargate tasks, as it does for EC2 instances.
traps.truth: Tasks in awsvpc mode are associated with a network interface, not an instance, so the target type must be ip.

traps.belief: ECS service auto scaling also adds and removes the EC2 instances of the cluster.
traps.truth: Service auto scaling changes the desired number of tasks; EC2 instances follow only through cluster auto scaling, the managed scaling of an Auto Scaling group capacity provider.

speak.prompt: ECS or EKS? My one Kubernetes engineer says that EKS is the standard.

plan.ten_second: Both run your containers, and both work with Fargate. EKS fits teams that already run Kubernetes; ECS is less to operate for you.
key_points_must: Both orchestrate containers and both run on Fargate (fargate-whitepaper-own-kernel-for-ecs-and-eks).
EKS runs upstream Kubernetes, so existing manifests and tools work (eks-faq-runs-open-source-kubernetes-compatible).
EKS has a per cluster per hour fee; ECS has no additional charge (eks-pricing-per-cluster-per-hour-fee, ecs-faq-no-additional-charge).
Skills decide: Kubernetes needs a team that handles frequent cluster upgrades (eks-decision-guide-kubernetes-skills-sre-teams).
key_points_nice: A Kubernetes version gets 14 months of standard support, then extended support at extra cost (eks-standard-support-14-months, eks-pricing-extended-support-additional-cost-per-cluster-hour).
must_not_say: error: 'ECS is not for production; EKS is the standard on AWS.' correct: ECS is a fully managed container orchestration service (ecs-fully-managed-orchestration).
error: 'With EKS we would run the Kubernetes control plane ourselves.' correct: EKS manages the control plane for you (eks-managed-control-plane-across-azs).
follow_ups: Can we move from ECS to EKS later? Yes: the same images in Amazon ECR work with both (ecr-faq-integrated-with-ecs-eks-lambda); only the task definitions become Kubernetes manifests.
Does Fargate Spot work with EKS? No: Amazon EKS does not support Fargate Spot (eks-fargate-no-spot); EKS uses Spot Instances in node groups.
plan.in_your_case: One Kubernetes engineer and six services: ECS on Fargate. Check-back question: 'Who would handle the cluster upgrades if your Kubernetes engineer is away?'

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Should we run our containers on Fargate or on EC2 instances? We want low cost and little operations work.

plan.ten_second: Start on Fargate: no instances to patch, and you pay per second for what each task asks for. Move to EC2 for GPUs or large steady fleets.
key_points_must: Fargate removes instance provisioning and scaling (fargate-no-provision-vm-clusters).
Fargate bills the requested vCPU and memory per second (ecs-faq-fargate-billing-granularity).
EC2 capacity fits control, GPUs and large price-optimized workloads (ecs-ec2-capacity-large-workloads-price-optimized, fargate-faq-gpu-not-supported).
Fargate Spot and Compute Savings Plans lower the Fargate bill (fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount, fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda).
must_not_say: error: 'Fargate always costs more than EC2.' correct: no AWS page says so; on Fargate you pay for what you provision (fargate-guide-pricing-per-second-pay-for-what-you-provision).
error: 'Fargate can run GPU work too.' correct: GPU workloads are not supported on Fargate today (fargate-faq-gpu-not-supported).
follow_ups: What happens when a Fargate Spot task is stopped? It gets a two-minute warning as SIGTERM, and the container must save its work (fargate-spot-warning-delivery-sigterm-eventbridge, fargate-spot-container-must-handle-sigterm).

Does a Savings Plan cover Fargate? Compute Savings Plans do (fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda); EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to an instance family (ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).

diagrams.title: One request through an ECS service on Fargate
diagrams.claim: An ECS service runs tasks from an ECR image on Fargate, and the load balancer sends each request to one task.
diagrams.alt: A VPC with private subnets in two Availability Zones. An Application Load Balancer sends requests to the Fargate tasks of one ECS service. The tasks pull their image from Amazon ECR and write to Amazon S3.
say: The ECS service starts tasks on Fargate, and Fargate will try its best to spread tasks across Availability Zones.
The task execution role grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents permission to pull the image from Amazon ECR.
The awsvpc mode provides each task with an elastic network interface, and the load balancer sends each request to one task.
The task role lets the application use other AWS services, such as Amazon S3.
